text: The applicants' details are set out in the appended table.
The respondent state is the Russian Government.
The facts of the case, as submitted by the parties, may be summarised as follows.
On 4 December 2011, general elections to the State Duma took place in Russia.
On 5 December 2011, the applicants participated in a public event in Moscow.
The applicants participated in the public event in Moscow to protest against the elections.
The applicants considered the elections to the State Duma held on 4 December 2011 to be rigged.
The authorities had been duly notified about the assembly held on 5 December 2011 in Moscow.

The circumstances relating to the public event of 5 December 2011 in Moscow have already been examined by the Court in Navalnyy and Yashin v. Russia, no. 76204/11, §§ 6-11, judgment of 4 December 2014.
After the demonstration on 5 December 2011, the applicants were arrested.
After being arrested, the applicants were transferred to various police stations in Moscow.
At the various police stations in Moscow, the relevant administrative records were drawn up in respect of the applicants.
The administrative offence records were based on the reports and explanations of the police officers who had arrested the applicants.
The applicants were detained at the relevant police stations.
The applicants spent up to three nights at the relevant police stations before being brought before the Justices of the Peace.
The applicants submitted that they had had no place to sleep during their detention at the police stations.
The applicants submitted that access to toilets had been restricted during their detention at the police stations.
Some of the applicants submitted that during transport to the place of detention following their administrative conviction, they had been kept for several hours in an unheated bus.
On various dates, all the applicants were convicted under Article 19.3 § 1 of the Code of Administrative Offences, which concerns refusal to obey the lawful order of a police officer.
The applicants were sentenced to either administrative fines or administrative imprisonment, as set out in the appended table.
The domestic courts relied on the administrative offence records when convicting the applicants.
The domestic courts relied on the reports and explanations of the police officers when convicting the applicants.
The domestic courts considered it unlawful that some of the applicants had shouted slogans during a public assembly that followed the initial demonstration.
The domestic courts considered it unlawful that some of the applicants had refused to stop participating in a public assembly that followed the initial demonstration.
The public assembly that followed the initial demonstration was one in respect of which no advance notification had been submitted to the authorities.
The relevant domestic law applicable at the material time is set out in Navalnyy and Yashin v. Russia, no. 76204/11, §§ 43-44, judgment of 4 December 2014.
